issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette:
Mai had always been the one in control. As a project manager, her job was to foresee obstacles, manage timelines, and steer complex initiatives to a calm, orderly conclusion. This sense of competence had defined her life until eight months ago, when her body had suddenly betrayed her. A routine infection had spiralled into septic shock, landing her in the ICU for two weeks. She remembered very little of that time with any coherence. What remained was a collage of disjointed sensations: the profound, bone-deep cold that no blanket could touch, the sharp, sterile scent of antiseptic that seemed to cling to the back of her throat, and the recurring image of an IV drip stand by her bed, its bag a clear, indifferent eye watching over her.

Her physical recovery was declared a success, but Mai felt fundamentally altered. The world, once manageable, was now seeded with threats. A blast of cold air from the office air conditioning could trigger a wave of panic so intense she’d have to retreat to her car. This sudden sensory assault would often bring with it a fragment of memory—not a story, but a raw, emotional echo of the terror she’d felt in the hospital, a feeling that would wash over her without any clear image attached. Because these memories were so sensory and unpredictable—a feeling of cold, a phantom smell—she found herself becoming hyper-aware of her physical surroundings, constantly on guard for the next assault on her senses. In response to these moments, she began a campaign of quiet avoidance. She started working from home more frequently, citing efficiency, but the truth was she couldn’t bear the building’s aggressive climate control or the smell of the industrial cleaning products used by the night crew. These triggers sent her fleeing, and she learned to evade them by shrinking her world.

This avoidance was part of a larger, desperate effort to regain control over her own mind. Mai had become convinced that the trauma had irrevocably broken her. The memory itself felt like proof; it was so extreme, so cinematic in its horror, that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her. This sense of unreality only strengthened her belief that her life, as she knew it, was over. The memory’s disjointed nature, with some moments of piercing clarity and others of complete blankness, felt less like a recollection and more like a symptom of a fracturing mind. The more she held the belief that she was permanently damaged, the more the memory seemed to confirm it, its strangeness a testament to her own.

These negative appraisals became the lens through which she saw everything. A simple trigger, like seeing a needle during a flu shot commercial, would not just startle her; it would send a jolt of confirmation through her: My body is weak, it failed me, it will fail me again. This conviction that she was physically vulnerable would, in turn, drag her back to the unreal quality of the ICU memory, replaying the thought that something so bizarre must have left a permanent scar on her very being. To escape this loop, she tried to consciously erase the event, pushing any thought of it away the moment it arose. But this strategy only made the memory more powerful and fragmented. The more she fought it, the more it would intrude as a disembodied feeling of dread or a single, sharp image, confirming her deepest fear that she was losing her mind. She began to constantly monitor her own thoughts, searching for any sign of "going crazy," a hypervigilance which, paradoxically, made her feel more unhinged and cemented her belief that she had failed in her most important roles—as a manager, a wife, and a mother. Her constant avoidance of medical cues had also made her even more attuned to spotting a syringe on a pharmacy poster from across the street.

The breaking point came last month. Her son had a routine check-up, and the thought of the doctor’s office—the smells, the equipment, the potential for a needle—was so overwhelming that she couldn’t bring herself to take him. Her husband had to leave work to handle it, and the look of confusion and concern on his face solidified her sense of failure. It was no longer a private struggle. She had come to therapy because she felt she was failing her family, her career, and herself. She feels trapped in a cycle of fear she cannot seem to think her way out of, and her greatest hope is simply to once again feel real in her own life.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself influences or creates new triggers for the patient.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
